title: Scaling writes: hardware and database choice
seriesDescription: How to scale write-heavy systems in an interview: vertical scaling and database choice, sharding and partition keys, vertical partitioning, queues and load shedding, batching, hierarchical aggregation, and the resharding and hot-key deep dives.
description: Exhausting vertical scaling, why append-only stores write fast, and how to tune a database for write-heavy workloads.
source: Study notes: the scaling writes pattern

questions.prompt: Writes are bottlenecked by which resources?

options.text: Disk I/O, CPU or network bandwidth, which you should confirm before changing architecture.
options.why: Right: find the wall you are hitting.

options.text: Only the colour of the dashboard without any extra configuration.
options.why: Not a real bottleneck.

options.text: The number of tables, regardless of load in a typical production setup.
options.why: Table count is not the limit.

options.text: The client browser version in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Unrelated to server write capacity.

questions.explanation: A quick calculation of actual throughput versus hardware capability shows whether you are near a limit.

questions.prompt: Why mention modern hardware (for example 200 cores and 10 Gbit networking) in an interview?

options.text: To show you did not add complexity when bigger hardware would do.
options.why: Right: avoid premature architecture.

options.text: Because interviewers never accept hardware as an answer in a typical production setup.
options.why: Many appreciate it, though some move the goalposts.

options.text: Because 4-core machines cannot run databases for most everyday workloads.
options.why: They can; the point is range.

options.text: To avoid discussing sharding forever.
options.why: Sharding often still comes up.

questions.explanation: Make the case, but do not argue if the interviewer wants to move on.

questions.prompt: Why can Cassandra sustain such high write rates?

options.text: It appends to a commit log sequentially instead of updating data in place with disk seeks.
options.why: Right: sequential writes are cheap.

options.text: It keeps all data only in memory and never writes to disk under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: It persists to disk through a commit log.

options.text: It has no replication, so there is less to write in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: It replicates; that is not the reason.

options.text: It rejects any write that needs an index.
options.why: It is not defined by rejecting writes.

questions.explanation: The trade-off is read performance: reads may check several files and merge results.

questions.prompt: Select all store types that favour high-volume writes in this pattern.

options.text: Time-series databases such as InfluxDB or TimescaleDB.
options.why: Yes: built for sequential timestamped writes.

options.text: Log-structured stores such as LevelDB.
options.why: Yes: they append instead of updating in place.

options.text: Column stores such as ClickHouse for analytics batches.
options.why: Yes: they batch writes efficiently.

options.text: A fully normalised database with many triggers and foreign keys.
options.why: No: that adds work to every write.

questions.explanation: Choose a specialised store only if the write volume justifies architecting around it.

questions.prompt: Which change makes a general-purpose database faster for writes?

options.text: Reducing index overhead, since every index must be updated on each write.
options.why: Right: fewer indexes, faster writes.

options.text: Adding an index to every column.
options.why: That slows writes down.

options.text: Turning on every trigger and constraint under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That adds per-write cost.

options.text: Running full-text indexing on every insert in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: That is expensive during high-write periods.

questions.explanation: You pay for it on reads, so know your access patterns first.

questions.prompt: True or false: tuning write-ahead logging so the database batches several transactions before flushing can improve write throughput.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: batching flushes reduces disk work.

options.text: False
options.why: It does help; flushes are the common bottleneck.

questions.explanation: Disk flush is the usual bottleneck, so amortising it across transactions helps, at some durability cost.

questions.prompt: Which statement best justifies choosing a faster write store?

options.text: Append-only writes avoid the in-place B-tree updates a relational database performs.
options.why: Right: name the mechanism.

options.text: It is a faster database without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: Too vague: explain why.

options.text: NoSQL always scales better than SQL as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: A broad claim without nuance.

options.text: Everybody uses it.
options.why: Popularity is not a technical reason.

questions.explanation: Do not say "use a faster database"; explain why it is faster and what you give up.
